option_description: Controls whether the Kubernetes API server accepts unauthenticated HTTP requests by processing them under the system:anonymous identity. Set via the --anonymous-auth flag on the kube-apiserver process. When true, any client that does not present credentials is still permitted to reach the API server and may access resources permitted to system:anonymous or system:unauthenticated groups.
security_impact: Directly triggers the unauthenticated_api_server_ingress rule when true. The Rego policy fires on two independent conditions involving this attribute: (1) anonymous_auth_enabled == true AND workload_to_apiserver_network_policy_enforced is false, and (2) anonymous_auth_enabled == true AND mutual_tls_enforced is false. In practice, most clusters lack one or both compensating controls, meaning enabling anonymous auth almost universally results in an exposure finding mapped to T1550.001 and T1599. The system:anonymous identity can be granted RBAC permissions deliberately or accidentally, and the attack surface is reachable by any pod that can route to port 6443.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the live kube-apiserver process arguments on the control plane node to check whether --anonymous-auth is present and its value.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o -- '--anonymous-auth=[^ ]*'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns '--anonymous-auth=false' for a hardened cluster. No output means the flag is absent; in Kubernetes 1.20+ the default is true when omitted, so absence is equivalent to true unless overridden by admission defaults.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Read the kube-apiserver static pod manifest directly from the control plane node filesystem and search for the anonymous-auth argument.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -i 'anonymous-auth' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A line such as '- --anonymous-auth=false' under the command or args section. Absence of the flag indicates the default (true) is in effect.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API server's /healthz/ping endpoint without credentials to confirm whether anonymous access is functionally enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk https://<API_SERVER_IP>:6443/api/v1/namespaces --max-time 5; echo "HTTP $?"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 401 Unauthorized response confirms anonymous auth is disabled or anonymous access is denied. A 200 or 403 response indicates unauthenticated requests are being processed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use kubectl to attempt a request as the anonymous user to verify effective RBAC posture for the system:anonymous subject.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl --as=system:anonymous auth can-i get pods -n default 2>&1
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'no' indicates anonymous users cannot list pods. Any affirmative response indicates RBAC permissions have been granted to the anonymous identity.

typical_values: true (default in Kubernetes; common in older or unconfigured clusters)
false (hardened deployments following CIS Benchmark 1.2.1)

option_description: Indicates whether Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources or an equivalent external firewall enforce that pods running in workload namespaces cannot initiate TCP connections to the API server endpoint (typically port 6443). A value of true means at least one enforcing policy is in place and the CNI plugin is capable of enforcing NetworkPolicy. A value of false means workload pods have unrestricted network-layer access to the API server.
security_impact: Acts as a compensating control in two unauthenticated_api_server_ingress Rego conditions. When anonymous_auth_enabled is true, the absence of this control (false) causes the first rule branch to fire. When api_server_insecure_port is greater than 0, the absence of this control causes the third rule branch to fire. Without network-layer restriction, any compromised workload pod can directly probe the API server, attempt credential brute-force, exploit unauthenticated endpoints, or target the insecure HTTP port. This corresponds to T1599 (Network Boundary Bridging) because the workload trust zone can reach the control plane trust zone without traversing a network enforcement point.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all NetworkPolicy resources across all namespaces and filter for egress rules that reference the API server port 6443 to identify whether any blocking policies exist.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.egress != null) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, egress: .spec.egress}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policies with egress rules containing 'ports: [{port: 6443}]' with no matching allow to the API server CIDR, or a default-deny egress policy in each workload namespace, confirm enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify whether the CNI plugin in the cluster enforces NetworkPolicy, since policies are no-ops without an enforcing CNI (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Weave). Check the DaemonSet or deployment in kube-system.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep -iE 'calico|cilium|weave|canal|antrea|flannel'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of Calico, Cilium, Antrea, or Canal pods indicates NetworkPolicy enforcement is available. Flannel alone does not enforce NetworkPolicy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a workload pod, attempt a TCP connection to the API server IP on port 6443 to validate whether the network policy is actually blocking the traffic at the data plane.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl run nettest --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- /bin/sh -c 'nc -zv <API_SERVER_IP> 6443; echo exit=$?'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused or timeout with exit code non-zero confirms enforcement. A successful TCP handshake (exit=0) confirms the policy is absent or not enforced by the CNI.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for a global egress deny-all NetworkPolicy in each workload namespace, which would block API server traffic unless explicitly allowed.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.podSelector == {} and .spec.egress == null and (.spec.policyTypes[]? == "Egress")) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of a namespace-scoped default-deny-egress policy in each workload namespace confirms that egress to the API server is blocked unless explicitly permitted.

typical_values: false (default; most clusters do not ship with workload-to-apiserver NetworkPolicy)
true (hardened multi-tenant clusters and CIS-compliant environments)

option_description: Controls whether the Kubernetes API server requires all clients to present a valid TLS certificate signed by a trusted CA, in addition to the server presenting its own certificate. Configured via the --client-ca-file flag on kube-apiserver. When true, both directions of the TLS handshake are authenticated, meaning clients without a valid certificate are rejected at the transport layer before any authentication plugin is consulted.
security_impact: Serves as a compensating control in the second branch of the unauthenticated_api_server_ingress Rego rule: when anonymous_auth_enabled is true AND mutual_tls_enforced is false, the exposure fires. Even when anonymous auth is technically enabled, mTLS prevents unauthenticated clients from reaching the API server because they cannot complete the TLS handshake without a valid client certificate. Without mTLS, bearer token theft, credential replay, and anonymous access all remain viable attack vectors. mTLS directly mitigates T1550.001 (Application Access Token abuse) by requiring a hardware-bound or PKI-bound credential rather than a bearer secret.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the live kube-apiserver process arguments on the control plane node to check whether --client-ca-file is set to a valid CA bundle path.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o -- '--client-ca-file=[^ ]*'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns '--client-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt' or equivalent path. Absence of this flag means client certificate authentication is not configured and mTLS is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Read the kube-apiserver static pod manifest and verify the --client-ca-file argument is present and points to an existing file.
how_to_obtain.command: grep 'client-ca-file' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml && ls -l $(grep 'client-ca-file' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | awk -F'=' '{print $2}')
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The grep returns the flag with a path and ls -l confirms the CA file exists and is readable. A missing file despite the flag being set would cause the API server to fail to start.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a TLS connection to the API server without providing a client certificate to determine whether the server enforces mutual authentication at the transport layer.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk --cacert /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt https://<API_SERVER_IP>:6443/api/v1/namespaces -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 400 (Bad Request) or a TLS alert indicating 'certificate required' confirms mTLS is enforced. HTTP 401 or 403 indicates the TLS handshake completed without a client cert, meaning mTLS is not enforced at the transport layer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the API server audit logs for requests authenticated as system:anonymous to determine whether unauthenticated connections are reaching the API layer, indicating mTLS is not enforced.
how_to_obtain.command: grep 'system:anonymous' /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero results suggests no anonymous access is reaching the API, consistent with mTLS or network-level blocking. Any results confirm clients are connecting without valid client certificates.

typical_values: false (default for service account and OIDC-only authentication setups)
true (kubeadm-provisioned clusters with --client-ca-file set; hardened CIS-compliant clusters)

option_description: Specifies the TCP port on which the kube-apiserver listens for plain HTTP (non-TLS) requests via the --insecure-port flag. When set to a non-zero value, the API server accepts requests on this port without TLS encryption and without requiring authentication or authorization, effectively bypassing all security middleware. A value of 0 disables the insecure listener entirely. The flag was deprecated in Kubernetes 1.20 and the default became 0.
security_impact: Directly triggers the third branch of the unauthenticated_api_server_ingress Rego rule when api_server_insecure_port > 0 AND workload_to_apiserver_network_policy_enforced is false. The insecure port bypasses authentication plugins, authorization modes (RBAC), and admission controllers entirely, meaning any client that can reach this port has unrestricted API access equivalent to cluster-admin. This is a critical T1599 (Network Boundary Bridging) risk because workload pods can reach cluster-administrative capability with a single unauthenticated HTTP request. Even with network policy, the flag's presence represents a severe misconfiguration risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the live kube-apiserver process arguments to check whether --insecure-port is set and its numeric value.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o -- '--insecure-port=[^ ]*'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: '--insecure-port=0' or no output confirms the insecure port is disabled. Any non-zero value (e.g., '--insecure-port=8080') indicates the insecure listener is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Read the kube-apiserver static pod manifest and search for the insecure-port argument to confirm its configured value.
how_to_obtain.command: grep 'insecure-port' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A line showing '- --insecure-port=0' is the secure configuration. Absence of the flag in Kubernetes 1.20+ defaults to 0. Any non-zero value is a critical finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt an unauthenticated HTTP connection to common insecure port values (8080, 8888) on the API server host to confirm whether the insecure listener is active.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s http://<API_SERVER_IP>:8080/api/v1/namespaces --max-time 5 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused or timeout (000) confirms the insecure port is not listening. HTTP 200 with a JSON API response confirms an active unauthenticated listener requiring immediate remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check listening TCP ports on the control plane node to identify whether any non-6443 ports associated with the kube-apiserver process are accepting connections.
how_to_obtain.command: ss -tlnp | grep kube-apiserver
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only port 6443 (or configured secure port) should appear. Presence of port 8080 or any other port bound by kube-apiserver confirms the insecure port is active.

typical_values: 0 (correct; default in Kubernetes 1.20+ and hardened clusters)
8080 (legacy default in Kubernetes < 1.20; still seen in older on-premises deployments)

option_description: Categorizes which network interfaces the etcd data store is bound to, derived from the --listen-client-urls and --listen-peer-urls flags. 'control_plane_only' means etcd is bound to loopback (127.0.0.1) or a dedicated control plane network interface not reachable from node or workload networks. 'node_network' means etcd is bound to an interface reachable from Kubernetes worker nodes. 'all_interfaces' means etcd is bound to 0.0.0.0 and is reachable from any network segment including workload pods.
security_impact: Controls which of two etcd_exposed_outside_control_plane_zone Rego rule branches fire. When etcd_listen_address_scope is 'all_interfaces' or 'node_network' AND firewall_restricts_etcd_to_control_plane is false, the exposure is raised. etcd contains the entire cluster state including secrets, service account tokens, and TLS certificates in base64-encoded form (or plaintext if encryption-at-rest is not configured). Direct etcd access bypasses the API server's authentication, authorization, and audit logging entirely. This maps to T1040 (Network Sniffing) and T1599 (Network Boundary Bridging) because an attacker on the node network can read all cluster secrets directly from the etcd client port 2379.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the live etcd process arguments to determine what address is bound for client connections via --listen-client-urls.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep etcd | grep -o -- '--listen-client-urls=[^ ]*'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: '--listen-client-urls=https://127.0.0.1:2379' maps to control_plane_only. An IP matching a node-network CIDR maps to node_network. 'https://0.0.0.0:2379' maps to all_interfaces.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the etcd static pod manifest or systemd unit file to read the configured listen URLs for client and peer communication.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'listen-client-urls|listen-peer-urls' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as '--listen-client-urls=https://127.0.0.1:2379,https://<CONTROL_PLANE_IP>:2379' confirm control_plane_only scope if the IP is on a dedicated control plane segment. Presence of 0.0.0.0 confirms all_interfaces.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a worker node, attempt a TCP connection to the control plane node on etcd client port 2379 to determine whether the etcd listener is reachable from the node network.
how_to_obtain.command: nc -zv <CONTROL_PLANE_IP> 2379 -w 3; echo exit=$?
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused or timeout (exit=1) from a worker node confirms etcd is bound only to the control plane network or loopback. Successful connection (exit=0) confirms node_network or all_interfaces scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the etcd host, verify which local interfaces are actually listening on port 2379 using ss to cross-check the configured URL scope.
how_to_obtain.command: ss -tlnp sport = :2379
how_to_obtain.expected_output: '127.0.0.1:2379' or a specific control plane IP listening confirms control_plane_only. '0.0.0.0:2379' confirms all_interfaces and is a critical finding requiring immediate firewall review.

typical_values: control_plane_only (kubeadm default; loopback + control plane IP)
node_network (some bare-metal and custom deployments exposing etcd to node CIDR)
all_interfaces (legacy or misconfigured deployments with 0.0.0.0 binding)

option_description: Indicates whether host-level firewall rules (iptables, nftables, firewalld) or network-level controls (cloud security groups, hardware firewall ACLs) enforce that etcd client port 2379 and peer port 2380 accept inbound TCP connections only from IP addresses within the control plane network segment. A value of true means an explicit allow rule limited to control plane source CIDRs exists and a default-deny or implicit-deny covers all other sources.
security_impact: Acts as the compensating control checked in both branches of the etcd_exposed_outside_control_plane_zone Rego rule. When this is false and etcd_listen_address_scope is 'node_network' or 'all_interfaces', the exposure fires because network-layer enforcement is absent. Even if etcd_client_cert_auth_enabled provides some authentication-layer defense (assessed as contextual evidence), the Rego rule does not treat it as a full substitute for network-zone enforcement. Firewall restriction is the primary defense-in-depth layer that enforces zone separation at the network boundary, directly addressing T1040 and T1599 by preventing non-control-plane hosts from establishing TCP sessions to etcd regardless of credential possession.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect iptables INPUT chain rules on the etcd host to verify whether rules explicitly restrict port 2379 and 2380 to control plane source CIDRs.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v --line-numbers | grep -E '2379|2380'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules of the form 'ACCEPT tcp -- <CONTROL_PLANE_CIDR> anywhere tcp dpt:2379' followed by a DROP or REJECT default confirm restriction. Absence of any etcd-specific rules with only a broad ACCEPT policy confirms the control is not in place.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check nftables rulesets on the etcd host as an alternative or replacement for iptables on modern Linux distributions.
how_to_obtain.command: nft list ruleset | grep -A 5 -B 5 '2379\|2380'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An nftables rule accepting traffic on ports 2379/2380 only from a specific control plane IP set, with a default policy of drop, confirms enforcement. No output indicates nftables is not managing etcd port restrictions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud-hosted control planes, use the cloud provider CLI to inspect security group or firewall rules associated with the etcd or control plane instances.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=group-id,Values=<SG_ID> --query 'SecurityGroups[].IpPermissions[?FromPort==`2379`]' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A rule permitting port 2379 only from a specific CIDR matching the control plane subnet (e.g., 10.0.1.0/24) confirms cloud-level restriction. An entry with 0.0.0.0/0 as the source CIDR is a critical finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the infrastructure-as-code or configuration management repository (Terraform, Ansible, CloudFormation) to confirm that etcd security group or firewall rules are defined as code and restrict source CIDRs to the control plane segment.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r '2379\|2380' <IaC_REPO_PATH> | grep -iE 'cidr|source|allow'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: IaC definitions referencing control plane CIDR blocks as permitted sources for ports 2379 and 2380, with no wildcard (0.0.0.0/0) sources, confirm the control is codified and enforced.

typical_values: true (managed Kubernetes services like EKS, GKE, AKS where control plane is fully isolated)
false (self-managed or bare-metal clusters without explicit firewall configuration)

option_description: An array containing the distinct subject kinds (e.g., 'ServiceAccount', 'User', 'Group') referenced in a ClusterRoleBinding's subjects list. This attribute identifies whether workload-level identity types such as ServiceAccounts, which operate within the lower workload trust zone, are being granted cluster-wide RBAC roles that provide administrative-level access across the control plane trust boundary. The presence of 'ServiceAccount' in this array is the key signal evaluated by the overpermissive_rbac_cluster_role_binding rule.
security_impact: The overpermissive_rbac_cluster_role_binding Rego rule evaluates five conditions, all requiring 'ServiceAccount' to be present in bound_subject_types combined with the subject namespace not being a system namespace. The specific privilege escalation paths checked are: wildcard verbs on wildcard resources, list access to secrets, create access to nodes, wildcard verbs on pods, and get access on wildcard resources. ServiceAccounts in workload namespaces receiving ClusterRoleBindings collapse the trust boundary because the SA token is mounted into pods (potentially via automountServiceAccountToken) and can be used by any process in that pod to perform cluster-administrative operations. This directly maps to T1098.006 (Additional Container Cluster Roles) and T1548.005 (Temporary Elevated Cloud Access).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all ClusterRoleBindings and extract the distinct subject kinds to populate this attribute, focusing on entries that include ServiceAccount subjects.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $name | .subjects[]? | select(.kind == "ServiceAccount") | [$name, .kind, .name, .namespace] | @csv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CSV rows showing ClusterRoleBinding name, kind (ServiceAccount), SA name, and namespace. Any ServiceAccount in a non-system namespace (not kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease) bound to a ClusterRole warrants further inspection of granted verbs and resources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify ClusterRoleBindings where ServiceAccounts from workload namespaces are bound to high-privilege ClusterRoles such as cluster-admin, edit, or custom roles with broad permissions.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.kind == "ServiceAccount") | {binding: .metadata.name, role: .roleRef.name, subjects: [.subjects[] | select(.kind == "ServiceAccount") | {name: .name, namespace: .namespace}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects showing ClusterRoleBindings with their role reference and ServiceAccount subjects including namespaces. Entries with role 'cluster-admin' or roles with wildcard rules are critical findings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For each ClusterRoleBinding found with ServiceAccount subjects in workload namespaces, inspect the associated ClusterRole to enumerate the specific verbs and resources granted.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrole <ROLE_NAME> -o json | jq '.rules[] | {verbs: .verbs, resources: .resources, apiGroups: .apiGroups}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules containing verbs: ['*'] or resources: ['*'] are highest risk. Rules with 'secrets'/'list' or 'nodes'/'create' match specific Rego rule branches triggering the overpermissive_rbac_cluster_role_binding exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Kubernetes API directly to retrieve ClusterRoleBindings with label or field selectors, useful in automated scanning pipelines or when kubectl RBAC is limited.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://kubernetes.default.svc/apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1/clusterrolebindings | jq '.items[].subjects[]? | select(.kind == "ServiceAccount")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of ServiceAccount subjects with name and namespace fields. Results with namespace values outside system namespaces (kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease) indicate workload-level identities with cluster-wide bindings requiring immediate review.

typical_values: ['ServiceAccount'] (workload service accounts with cluster-level bindings; common in improperly scoped Helm charts)
['User'] (human or external identity bindings; typical for developer or operator access)
['Group'] (group-based bindings; common for OIDC or LDAP-integrated clusters)
['ServiceAccount', 'User'] (mixed bindings; seen in clusters with both automated workloads and human operator RBAC in the same ClusterRoleBinding)

option_description: Controls which action verbs (e.g., get, list, watch, create, update, delete, '*') are explicitly authorized by a ClusterRole referenced in a ClusterRoleBinding. Defines the operational surface a bound service account may exercise against Kubernetes API resources.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags bindings where '*' appears in granted_verbs combined with sensitive resources, or where specific dangerous verbs like 'list' on secrets or 'create' on nodes are present. A wildcard verb grant on any resource, or targeted dangerous verbs on secrets/pods/nodes, triggers the overpermissive_rbac_cluster_role_binding exposure, enabling a compromised workload identity to escalate to cluster-wide administrative control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve all ClusterRoleBindings and extract their referenced ClusterRole names, then dump the rules including verbs for each ClusterRole.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .roleRef.name' | sort -u | xargs -I{} kubectl get clusterrole {} -o json 2>/dev/null | jq '.rules[].verbs'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON arrays of verb strings per ClusterRole rule, e.g., ["get","list","watch"] or ["*"]

how_to_obtain.instruction: Directly inspect a specific ClusterRole by name and extract its verb grants from all rules.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrole <role-name> -o jsonpath='{range .rules[*]}{.verbs}{"\n"}{end}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One line per rule showing the verbs array; wildcard '*' entries indicate overpermissive grants.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all ClusterRoles that contain wildcard verbs or dangerous specific verbs in a single scan.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.rules[]?.verbs[]? | . == "*" or . == "create" or . == "list") | .metadata.name'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of ClusterRole names that contain '*', 'create', or 'list' verbs — these warrant deeper binding review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API server directly to retrieve ClusterRole rules and inspect verb grants programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://${KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST}/apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1/clusterroles/<role-name> | jq '.rules[].verbs'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON arrays of verbs for each rule in the ClusterRole definition.

typical_values: ["get", "list", "watch"]
["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
["list"]
["create"]

option_description: Defines which Kubernetes resource types (e.g., secrets, pods, nodes, configmaps, '*') are explicitly granted by a ClusterRole rule. Determines the resource scope a bound identity may act upon across the cluster.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the overpermissive_rbac_cluster_role_binding exposure when 'secrets' appears in granted_resources with 'list' verb, when 'nodes' appears with 'create', when 'pods' appears with wildcard verbs, or when '*' (wildcard resource) is combined with any sensitive verb. Broad or wildcard resource grants dramatically expand blast radius if a workload identity is compromised, collapsing the workload-to-control-plane trust boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all resources granted by every ClusterRole currently in the cluster.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq -r '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, resources: [.rules[].resources // [] | .[]] } | select(.resources | length > 0)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects mapping ClusterRole names to their flattened resource lists; entries containing '*' or 'secrets' require immediate review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all ClusterRoles that grant access to high-risk resource types: secrets, nodes, pods, or wildcard.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.rules[]?.resources[]? | . == "secrets" or . == "nodes" or . == "*") | .metadata.name'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Names of ClusterRoles granting access to secrets, nodes, or wildcard resources — these must be cross-referenced against their bindings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the resources for a specific ClusterRole referenced by a binding.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrole <role-name> -o json | jq '.rules[] | {resources: .resources, verbs: .verbs}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects per rule showing resource-verb pairs; sensitive combinations like secrets+list or nodes+create indicate escalation risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the RBAC API endpoint to retrieve ClusterRole resource grants for automated compliance scanning.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterroles -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{range .rules[*]}{.resources}{"\n"}{end}{end}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Multi-line output pairing ClusterRole names with their resource arrays for each rule.

typical_values: ["pods"]
["secrets"]
["nodes"]
["pods", "deployments", "services"]
["configmaps", "secrets", "serviceaccounts"]

option_description: Identifies the namespace of the ServiceAccount subject referenced in a ClusterRoleBinding or RoleBinding. Determines whether a workload-zone identity is receiving cluster-scoped privileges or cross-tenant access that violates horizontal trust zone separation.
security_impact: The Rego policy checks subject_namespace against a safe list of system namespaces (kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease). If the subject's namespace falls outside this list, any broad verb or sensitive resource grant triggers the overpermissive_rbac_cluster_role_binding exposure. The attribute also directly triggers the cross_tenant_namespace_rbac_propagation exposure when a non-null subject_namespace is present in a cross-binding context, indicating trust zone boundary crossing via RBAC propagation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all ClusterRoleBinding subjects that are ServiceAccounts and display their namespaces alongside the ClusterRole they are bound to.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | {binding: .metadata.name, role: .roleRef.name, subjects: [.subjects[]? | select(.kind=="ServiceAccount") | {name: .name, namespace: .namespace}]} | select(.subjects | length > 0)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects listing binding name, referenced ClusterRole, and subject ServiceAccount names with their namespaces; non-system namespaces paired with sensitive ClusterRoles are the priority finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Specifically identify ClusterRoleBindings where ServiceAccount subjects originate from non-system namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | .kind=="ServiceAccount" and (.namespace | . != "kube-system" and . != "kube-public" and . != "kube-node-lease")) | .metadata.name + " -> " + .subjects[].namespace'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of ClusterRoleBinding names with the non-system namespace of their ServiceAccount subjects — each represents a potential cross-boundary privilege grant.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check RoleBindings for cross-tenant subjects where a ServiceAccount from a foreign namespace is referenced.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get rolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | {binding_ns: .metadata.namespace, binding: .metadata.name, foreign_subjects: [.subjects[]? | select(.kind=="ServiceAccount" and .namespace != null and .namespace != .parent)]} | select(.foreign_subjects | length > 0)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RoleBindings that reference ServiceAccounts from namespaces other than where the binding resides, indicating cross-tenant RBAC propagation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the cluster's namespace-to-team/tenant mapping documentation to identify which namespaces represent workload trust zones vs. administrative zones, and verify that ClusterRoleBindings do not grant cluster-wide privileges to workload-zone service accounts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A confirmed mapping of namespace names to trust zone designations, enabling accurate classification of subject_namespace values as safe (system) or risky (workload/tenant).

option_description: Controls the behavior of an admission webhook when its endpoint is unreachable or returns an error. 'Fail' causes the API server to reject the admission request; 'Ignore' allows the request to proceed as if the webhook approved it, creating a fail-open condition.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers both the admission_webhook_bypass_via_missing_coverage and admission_webhook_failure_open_policy exposures when webhook_failure_policy equals 'Ignore'. A fail-open policy means any disruption to the webhook service — including targeted denial-of-service, network partition, or pod crash — creates an unguarded ingress path through the admission control boundary. Attackers can deliberately cause webhook failures to deploy workloads that would otherwise be denied by OPA/Gatekeeper, Kyverno, or image validation policies.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate failurePolicy settings across all ValidatingWebhookConfigurations and MutatingWebhookConfigurations.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{range .webhooks[*]}{.name}{" failurePolicy="}{.failurePolicy}{"\n"}{end}{end}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines pairing webhook names with their failurePolicy values; any 'Ignore' entry on a security-enforcing webhook is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Filter to only show webhooks explicitly configured with the fail-open 'Ignore' policy.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $cfg | .webhooks[]? | select(.failurePolicy == "Ignore") | $cfg + "/" + .name + ": Ignore"'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of configuration/webhook name pairs with 'Ignore' policy; empty output is the desired secure state for security-enforcing webhooks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If webhooks are deployed via Helm charts or static manifests, inspect the webhook configuration YAML files for the failurePolicy field.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'failurePolicy' /path/to/webhook-manifests/ --include='*.yaml' -A 1
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing failurePolicy values in source manifests; 'Ignore' in security-critical webhook definitions indicates a configuration debt requiring remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API directly to retrieve webhook configurations and their failure policies.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, webhooks: [.webhooks[] | {webhook: .name, failurePolicy: .failurePolicy}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Structured JSON per webhook configuration showing each webhook's name and failurePolicy; 'Fail' is the secure expected value for policy-enforcing webhooks.

typical_values: Ignore
Fail

option_description: Indicates whether a webhook's namespaceSelector configuration excludes kube-system, kube-public, or other privileged system namespaces from policy enforcement coverage. When true, workloads deployed into these high-privilege namespaces bypass the admission webhook entirely.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the admission_webhook_bypass_via_missing_coverage exposure when this attribute is true. System namespaces like kube-system host critical cluster infrastructure. If an attacker gains the ability to deploy into kube-system (e.g., via a misconfigured RBAC binding), exempting these namespaces from admission webhooks means security policies (pod security standards, image validation, network policy injection) are not enforced there, enabling deployment of privileged or malicious workloads without policy interception.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the namespaceSelector of all webhooks to identify those that explicitly exclude kube-system or other privileged namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $cfg | .webhooks[]? | select(.namespaceSelector != null) | $cfg + "/" + .name + ": " + (.namespaceSelector | tostring)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Webhook names with their namespaceSelector definitions; look for matchExpressions using NotIn or DoesNotExist operators targeting 'kubernetes.io/metadata.name' with kube-system values.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether kube-system namespace has the label that would be required for webhook selection, and whether webhooks use matchLabels that would exclude it.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get namespace kube-system -o json | jq '.metadata.labels'; kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq '[.items[].webhooks[]?.namespaceSelector | select(. != null)]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The kube-system namespace labels alongside webhook selectors; if the webhook requires a label not present on kube-system, the namespace is effectively excluded.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify webhooks with no namespaceSelector (covers all namespaces) versus those with selectors that may exclude system namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $cfg | .webhooks[] | [$cfg, .name, (if .namespaceSelector == null then "NO_SELECTOR(all)" else (.namespaceSelector | tostring) end)] | join(" | ")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Tabular output showing each webhook's namespace selection behavior; 'NO_SELECTOR(all)' covers all namespaces, while complex selectors must be manually verified against system namespace labels.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the admission webhook deployment documentation or Helm values to determine if system namespace exclusion was intentionally configured and whether compensating controls exist for kube-system workload admission.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written justification for any system namespace exemptions, identifying whether they are intentional (e.g., bootstrapping requirements) and what compensating controls are in place.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Controls how the API server matches incoming resource requests against the webhook's rules. 'Equivalent' matches requests for a resource regardless of which API version is used (treating all versions as equivalent). 'Exact' only matches the specific API group/version/resource combinations explicitly listed, potentially missing requests made via alternate API versions.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the admission_webhook_bypass_via_missing_coverage exposure when webhook_match_policy equals 'Exact'. Kubernetes supports multiple API versions for many resources (e.g., apps/v1, apps/v1beta1, extensions/v1beta1 for deployments in older clusters). An attacker aware of the webhook's exact version restrictions can craft API requests using an unlisted but valid API version to bypass admission enforcement. 'Equivalent' is the default and closes this bypass path.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract matchPolicy settings from all admission webhook configurations.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{range .webhooks[*]}{.name}{" matchPolicy="}{.matchPolicy}{"\n"}{end}{end}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing webhook names with their matchPolicy; 'Exact' values should be flagged for review. Absence of matchPolicy implies the cluster default (Equivalent in Kubernetes 1.15+).

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all webhooks explicitly set to 'Exact' match policy.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.name as $cfg | .webhooks[]? | select(.matchPolicy == "Exact") | $cfg + "/" + .name + ": Exact (REVIEW REQUIRED)"'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Webhook entries using 'Exact' match policy — these must be cross-referenced with the API versions they cover to identify potential bypass paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the full webhook rules including API groups and versions to assess whether 'Exact' policy creates coverage gaps.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq '.items[] | {config: .metadata.name, webhooks: [.webhooks[] | {name: .name, matchPolicy: (.matchPolicy // "Equivalent"), rules: [.rules[] | {apiGroups: .apiGroups, apiVersions: .apiVersions, resources: .resources}]}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Structured JSON showing each webhook's match policy alongside its covered API groups/versions; 'Exact' webhooks covering only 'v1' of a resource but missing 'v1beta1' represent a concrete bypass vector.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect source webhook configuration manifests for matchPolicy declarations, particularly in OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno deployment manifests.
how_to_obtain.command: find /path/to/webhook-manifests -name '*.yaml' | xargs grep -l 'matchPolicy' | xargs grep -A 1 'matchPolicy'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: matchPolicy field values in source manifests; 'Exact' in security-critical webhook definitions should be changed to 'Equivalent' unless there is a documented reason for the restriction.

typical_values: Equivalent
Exact

option_description: Represents the set of high-risk Kubernetes resource types (pods, deployments, secrets, serviceaccounts, daemonsets, etc.) that are not covered by any admission webhook rule. Resources absent from all webhook rule definitions receive no policy enforcement and can be created or modified without admission control interception.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the admission_webhook_bypass_via_missing_coverage exposure when this array contains one or more entries. Any resource type not covered by a webhook — even if the webhook is otherwise correctly configured — represents a direct ingress path through the admission enforcement boundary. Attackers can create pods, modify RBAC bindings, or deploy workloads using the uncovered resource types to bypass security policies that would otherwise block their actions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract all resource types covered by current webhook rules and compare against a defined list of high-risk resources to identify gaps.
how_to_obtain.command: COVERED=$(kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '[.items[].webhooks[]?.rules[]?.resources[]?] | unique | .[]'); for r in pods deployments secrets serviceaccounts daemonsets statefulsets configmaps nodes clusterroles clusterrolebindings; do echo "$COVERED" | grep -qx "$r" || echo "UNCOVERED: $r"; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines prefixed 'UNCOVERED:' listing high-risk resource types not present in any webhook rule definition; each uncovered type is a policy enforcement gap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all resources covered across all webhook configurations in a single flattened view.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{range .webhooks[*]}{range .rules[*]}{.resources}{"\n"}{end}{end}{end}' | tr -d '[]"' | tr ',' '\n' | sort -u
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Sorted unique list of all resource types covered by at least one webhook rule; cross-reference manually against your high-risk resource inventory.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the full webhook rule definitions to perform detailed gap analysis including API groups.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq '[.items[].webhooks[]?.rules[]? | {apiGroups, apiVersions, resources, operations}] | unique'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array of unique rule definitions showing covered API groups, versions, resources, and operations; gaps in operations (missing CREATE, UPDATE) or resources indicate enforcement blind spots.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the security policy requirements document for the cluster to identify which resource types are mandated to be under admission control, then cross-reference with the discovered covered resource list to produce a formal gap analysis.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A gap matrix showing required vs. actually covered resource types, with each uncovered required resource documented as a finding requiring remediation.
