option_description: Controls whether Kubernetes automatically mounts the service account token as a volume into every pod in a namespace or for a specific pod spec. When true or unset (defaulting to true), the token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token is injected into every container, providing API server credentials to any process running inside the pod.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'service_account_token_auto_mount_across_trust_zones' exposure when automount_service_account_token is true AND either the service account has elevated RBAC permissions, or the pod runs in a 'restricted' or 'administrative' trust zone. Auto-mounting collapses the workload-to-control-plane trust boundary by distributing API credentials into lower-trust environments, enabling any compromised container to authenticate to the Kubernetes API without requiring explicit credential provisioning.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check all pod specs in a namespace for the automountServiceAccountToken field. Absent or true values indicate the token is mounted.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, automount: .spec.automountServiceAccountToken}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each pod entry shows automount as true, false, or null (null means defaulting to true unless overridden on the ServiceAccount).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect ServiceAccount objects to check their automountServiceAccountToken setting, which serves as the default for all pods using that account.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, automount: .automountServiceAccountToken}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ServiceAccount entries show automount as true, false, or null. A null value means pods default to mounting the token unless explicitly overridden at the pod level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for pods that actually have the service account token volume mounted as evidence of the token being injected.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]?.name == "kube-api-access" or .spec.volumes[]?.projected != null) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pods returned have projected service account token volumes actively mounted, confirming token injection is occurring.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API server directly to retrieve pod specs and service account configurations for automated auditing.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/pods | jq '[.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, ns: .metadata.namespace, automount: .spec.automountServiceAccountToken}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array with pod names and their automount settings; entries with null or true require remediation review.

typical_values: true (default when field is absent — majority of legacy deployments)
false (hardened deployments following CIS Kubernetes Benchmark)
null/absent (treated as true; most common in default service accounts)

option_description: Indicates whether the service account associated with the pod holds ClusterRole or Role bindings that grant permissions exceeding minimal read-only access, such as write verbs (create, update, delete, patch) or access to sensitive resources like secrets, nodes, pods, or clusterroles. This reflects the actual privilege scope a compromised pod could exercise against the Kubernetes API.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'service_account_token_auto_mount_across_trust_zones' when both automount_service_account_token is true AND this attribute is true, regardless of namespace trust zone. This combination means a compromised container immediately possesses API credentials with elevated cluster permissions, directly enabling privilege escalation and lateral movement across the control plane boundary. The policy also flags 'overpermissive_rbac_cluster_role_binding' for accounts with wildcard verbs or access to secrets/nodes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate ClusterRoleBindings and RoleBindings to identify service accounts with elevated RBAC permissions, checking for write verbs or sensitive resource access.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.kind == "ServiceAccount") | {binding: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, subjects: .subjects, roleRef: .roleRef}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of bindings referencing ServiceAccount subjects; cross-reference roleRef names against role definitions for write verbs or sensitive resources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use kubectl auth can-i to check if a specific service account can perform sensitive operations such as listing secrets or creating pods.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<serviceaccount-name> -n <namespace> && kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<serviceaccount-name>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'yes' responses indicate the service account holds elevated permissions that exceed read-only access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the specific ClusterRole or Role referenced by the service account's binding to enumerate all granted verbs and resources.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterrole <role-name> -o json | jq '.rules[] | {verbs: .verbs, resources: .resources, apiGroups: .apiGroups}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules with verbs like create, update, delete, patch, or * on resources like secrets, pods, nodes, or clusterroles indicate elevated RBAC permissions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use rakkess or kubectl-who-can to perform a broad sweep of which service accounts have write access to sensitive resources across the cluster.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl-who-can create secrets && kubectl-who-can delete pods && kubectl-who-can update clusterroles
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output lists all subjects including ServiceAccounts that have the queried permission; any service account appearing in workload namespaces is a finding.

typical_values: false (expected in hardened environments with least-privilege RBAC)
true (common in default installations, Helm-deployed applications, and CI/CD integrated service accounts)
true (frequently observed for monitoring agents like Prometheus with cluster-wide read access)

option_description: Represents the trust zone classification assigned to the Kubernetes namespace where the pod runs. Classifications indicate the sensitivity of the operational environment: 'restricted' for high-sensitivity production or PCI/HIPAA-scoped workloads, 'standard' for general production, 'administrative' for namespaces with control-plane-adjacent functions, and 'unclassified' for development or unknown environments.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'service_account_token_auto_mount_across_trust_zones' when automount is enabled and this zone is 'restricted' or 'administrative', even without confirmed elevated RBAC. This reflects that any API credential exposure in high-sensitivity zones represents unacceptable risk because tokens in these zones have elevated blast radius — compromise of a restricted or administrative namespace pod provides attackers with credentials in the most sensitive trust domain, potentially bypassing zone isolation controls.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect namespace labels to identify trust zone classification labels applied by organizational policy or security tooling.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, labels: .metadata.labels, annotations: .metadata.annotations}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Namespaces with trust zone labels such as 'security-zone=restricted', 'trust-level=administrative', or equivalent organizational conventions; unclassified namespaces lack these labels.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Look for Pod Security Admission labels which often correlate with trust zone classification (restricted and baseline profiles).
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, psa_enforce: .metadata.labels["pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce"], psa_warn: .metadata.labels["pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn"]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Namespaces with enforce=restricted typically map to 'restricted' trust zones; enforce=baseline maps to 'standard'; absent labels indicate 'unclassified'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review organizational namespace management documentation, internal wikis, or CMDB entries to determine the formal trust zone classification policy and which namespaces fall under each category.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review internal documentation at locations such as Confluence, SharePoint, or GitOps repository README files under /namespaces/ or /environments/ directories for trust zone assignments.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation mapping namespace names to trust zones (restricted, standard, administrative, unclassified) with criteria for each classification.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Examine namespace manifests in GitOps repositories for trust zone labels and annotations applied at provisioning time.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'trust-zone\|security-zone\|trust-level\|classification' /path/to/gitops-repo/namespaces/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: YAML manifests with metadata.labels entries indicating trust zone classification; absence of labels indicates 'unclassified' status.

typical_values: unclassified (default in most organizations lacking formal namespace classification)
standard (common for production application namespaces)
restricted (used for PCI, HIPAA, or other regulated workload namespaces)
administrative (assigned to namespaces housing operators, controllers, or cluster management tools)

option_description: Indicates whether any RoleBinding within a tenant namespace grants permissions to subjects (ServiceAccounts or Groups) whose namespace field references a different namespace than the one the RoleBinding resides in. This configuration represents cross-namespace RBAC propagation where one tenant's resources are explicitly granted access to another tenant's namespace.
security_impact: The Rego policy directly triggers 'cross_tenant_namespace_rbac_propagation' when this attribute is true, unconditionally. Cross-namespace subject references violate horizontal trust zone separation between tenants by creating implicit authorization tunnels between namespaces. An attacker who compromises a pod in namespace A that holds a foreign RoleBinding in namespace B can immediately act within namespace B's resource scope, collapsing the isolation boundary between tenants without any network-layer traversal.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all RoleBindings across all namespaces and identify any subject with a namespace field that differs from the RoleBinding's own namespace.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get rolebindings -A -o json | jq '.items[] | . as $rb | .subjects[]? | select(.kind == "ServiceAccount" and .namespace != $rb.metadata.namespace) | {rolebinding: $rb.metadata.name, rb_namespace: $rb.metadata.namespace, subject_name: .name, subject_namespace: .namespace}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any returned entries indicate foreign namespace subjects; an empty result means no cross-namespace RoleBinding subjects exist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Script a comprehensive check across all tenant namespaces, excluding system namespaces, to find cross-namespace RoleBinding subjects.
how_to_obtain.command:
for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' | tr ' ' '
' | grep -v '^kube-'); do kubectl get rolebindings -n $ns -o json 2>/dev/null | jq --arg ns "$ns" '.items[] | .subjects[]? | select(.kind == "ServiceAccount" and .namespace != null and .namespace != $ns) | {rolebinding_ns: $ns, subject: .}'; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects showing any RoleBinding namespace and the foreign subject details; empty output indicates no cross-namespace bindings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API for RoleBindings and programmatically compare subject namespaces against binding namespaces for comprehensive auditing.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://$APISERVER/apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1/rolebindings | jq '[.items[] | . as $rb | .subjects[]? | select(.kind == "ServiceAccount" and .namespace != null and .namespace != $rb.metadata.namespace) | {rb: $rb.metadata.name, rb_ns: $rb.metadata.namespace, subject_ns: .namespace}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of cross-namespace binding violations; empty array indicates compliant state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Helm chart templates and GitOps manifests that provision RoleBindings to determine if any templates include cross-namespace subject references by design.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'namespace:' /path/to/gitops-repo/ | grep -A2 -B2 'subjects' | grep -v 'metadata.namespace'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RoleBinding YAML sections where subjects[].namespace differs from metadata.namespace; these represent intentional cross-namespace grants requiring justification.

typical_values: false (expected baseline in properly segmented multi-tenant clusters)
true (common in clusters where shared services or operators are granted access across namespaces via RoleBindings rather than ClusterRoleBindings)
true (frequently introduced by Helm charts deploying operators that bind service accounts from the operator namespace into tenant namespaces)

option_description: Indicates whether any namespace-scoped Role object (as opposed to ClusterRole) within a tenant namespace contains rules that reference cluster-scoped Kubernetes resource types such as nodes, persistentvolumes, namespaces, clusterroles, or clusterrolebindings. Because Roles are namespace-scoped objects, including cluster-scoped resource references within them is either ineffective or represents a misconfiguration that can create confusion about the actual granted permissions.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'cross_tenant_namespace_rbac_propagation' when this attribute is true. Roles referencing cluster-scoped resources blur the boundary between namespace-scoped and cluster-scoped authorization. Even if the grants are technically ineffective for some cluster-scoped resources, their presence indicates RBAC design confusion that may allow privilege escalation through misinterpretation, and in some versions or configurations they may grant unintended cluster-wide access. Attackers can exploit this ambiguity to probe cluster-level resources from what appears to be a tenant-scoped role.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect all Role objects across tenant namespaces and check their rules for cluster-scoped resource kinds such as nodes, persistentvolumes, namespaces, clusterroles, and clusterrolebindings.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get roles -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.rules[].resources[]? | test("^(nodes|persistentvolumes|namespaces|clusterroles|clusterrolebindings|storageclasses|ingressclasses|runtimeclasses|priorityclasses)$")) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, rules: .rules}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Role objects whose rules array contains cluster-scoped resource types; empty output indicates no roles reference cluster-scoped resources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a broader audit of all Roles across non-system namespaces and output their full rule sets for manual review.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get roles -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.namespace | test("^kube-") | not) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, rules: [.rules[] | {resources: .resources, verbs: .verbs, apiGroups: .apiGroups}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Role rules per namespace; manually check resources arrays for node, persistentvolume, namespace, clusterrole, or clusterrolebinding entries.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use a targeted grep against GitOps YAML manifests to find Role definitions containing cluster-scoped resource references.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'kind: Role' /path/to/gitops-repo/ -l | xargs grep -l 'nodes\|persistentvolumes\|clusterroles\|namespaces\|storageclasses'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: File paths of Role manifests containing cluster-scoped resource references; these files require RBAC architecture review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes RBAC API for all Role objects and filter for cluster-scoped resource references programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://$APISERVER/apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1/roles | jq '[.items[] | select(.rules[].resources[]? | test("nodes|persistentvolumes|clusterroles|namespaces|clusterrolebindings")) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of Role names and namespaces containing cluster-scoped resource references; empty array indicates compliant state.

typical_values: false (expected in properly architected RBAC models where cluster-scoped resources are only referenced in ClusterRoles)
true (commonly introduced by automated RBAC generation tools or operators that incorrectly use Role instead of ClusterRole for cluster-scoped resource grants)
true (found in clusters where RBAC was migrated from older versions without reviewing resource scope changes)

option_description: An array listing the trust zones where kubeconfig files or service account tokens carrying cluster-admin or broad namespace rights are stored or accessible. Each entry represents a distinct environment category: 'ci_cd_runner' for pipeline execution environments, 'developer_workstation' for local development machines, 'workload_namespace' for Kubernetes pods, 'monitoring_agent' for observability infrastructure, and 'control_plane' for the trusted administrative zone where such credentials should ideally be confined.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'kubeconfig_credential_not_isolated_by_zone' when any of 'ci_cd_runner', 'developer_workstation', 'workload_namespace', or 'monitoring_agent' appear in this array AND credential_scope is 'cluster_admin' or 'broad_namespace'. Presence of high-privilege kubeconfig files in lower-trust zones means a single compromise of that zone (e.g., a CI/CD pipeline injection or developer workstation malware infection) immediately yields cluster-admin credentials, completely collapsing the control plane trust boundary without requiring any Kubernetes-layer exploitation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search CI/CD runner environments, shared storage, and secrets management systems for kubeconfig files with cluster-admin or broad namespace rights.
how_to_obtain.command: find / -name 'kubeconfig' -o -name '.kube' -type d 2>/dev/null | head -50 && find /home /root /etc /var/lib -name 'config' -path '*/.kube/*' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: File paths where kubeconfig files exist; each location represents a zone where credentials are stored and must be assessed against its trust classification.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview DevOps and platform engineering teams to identify all systems where cluster-admin kubeconfig files are provisioned, including CI/CD secrets, developer onboarding processes, and monitoring agent configurations.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review CI/CD platform secret stores (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab CI variables, Jenkins credentials store, Vault paths) for kubeconfig or KUBECONFIG entries. Check onboarding documentation for developer workstation credential provisioning steps.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An inventory of all zones where high-privilege kubeconfig files are provisioned, enabling mapping to: ci_cd_runner, developer_workstation, workload_namespace, monitoring_agent, or control_plane.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Audit Kubernetes Secrets across namespaces for stored kubeconfig content or service account tokens with elevated permissions.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get secrets -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.type == "kubernetes.io/service-account-token" or (.data | keys[] | test("kubeconfig|KUBECONFIG"))) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, type: .type}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secrets containing kubeconfig data or service account tokens stored in workload namespaces rather than control-plane-only namespaces indicate misplaced high-privilege credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Vault secret paths or AWS/GCP/Azure secrets manager for kubeconfig files accessible to CI/CD or workload zone IAM roles.
how_to_obtain.command: vault kv list secret/ | grep -i 'kubeconfig\|kube\|k8s' && vault read sys/audit
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Vault paths containing kubeconfig material accessible to non-control-plane roles; each path indicates a zone where credentials are stored.

typical_values: ['control_plane'] (ideal state — credentials confined to control plane zone only)
['ci_cd_runner', 'control_plane'] (common in automated deployment pipelines — requires risk acceptance or mitigation)
['ci_cd_runner', 'developer_workstation', 'control_plane'] (typical in organizations without formal credential zone policies)
['workload_namespace', 'monitoring_agent', 'ci_cd_runner', 'developer_workstation', 'control_plane'] (high-risk state indicating absent credential isolation)

option_description: Indicates whether pods or systems operating in workload namespaces or other lower-trust zones have network-reachable or API-level access to the credential store that holds control-plane-scoped kubeconfig files or service account tokens. This encompasses Vault instances, Kubernetes Secrets backing high-privilege credentials, CI/CD secret stores, or any other system storing cluster-admin or broad-namespace credentials.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'kubeconfig_credential_not_isolated_by_zone' when this is true AND credential_scope is 'cluster_admin' or 'broad_namespace'. This configuration creates a direct credential theft path: a workload-zone compromise (container breakout, RCE in a pod) gives an attacker network or API access to the credential store, from which they can retrieve cluster-admin credentials and achieve full control plane compromise. This effectively eliminates the trust boundary between workload and control plane zones by providing a credential extraction vector that bypasses authentication enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test network reachability from a workload pod to the Vault or credential store endpoint to determine if workload-zone processes can reach the credential store.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl run -it --rm nettest --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sh -c 'nc -zv <vault-host> 8200 && nc -zv <kube-apiserver> 6443'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Successful connections indicate the workload zone can reach credential stores; connections should be blocked by NetworkPolicy or firewall rules for a compliant posture.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect NetworkPolicy objects in workload namespaces to verify egress rules explicitly deny access to credential store endpoints (Vault, secrets backends).
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -A -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, spec: .spec}' && kubectl get networkpolicy -A --no-headers | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NetworkPolicies with egress deny rules covering Vault CIDR ranges and control-plane credential store ports; absence of such policies indicates workload zone can access credential stores.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Vault policies bound to Kubernetes auth roles for workload namespaces to determine if workload service accounts can authenticate to Vault and read high-privilege credential paths.
how_to_obtain.command: vault read auth/kubernetes/role/<workload-role-name> && vault policy read <associated-policy-name>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Vault policies granting read access to paths containing kubeconfig or cluster-admin service account tokens indicate workload-zone access to the credential store.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Kubernetes RBAC to check if workload service accounts can read Secrets in namespaces that store high-privilege kubeconfig content.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n kube-system --as=system:serviceaccount:<workload-namespace>:<workload-sa> && kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n <credential-namespace> --as=system:serviceaccount:<workload-namespace>:<workload-sa>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'yes' responses indicate the workload-zone service account can read credential store Secrets, confirming workload_zone_credential_store_accessible is true.

typical_values: false (compliant state with network segmentation and Vault policy scoping preventing workload zone access)
true (common when Vault is deployed cluster-internally without NetworkPolicy restricting workload egress to Vault)
true (frequently observed when all service accounts are granted read access to kube-system Secrets for convenience)
false (achieved through combination of NetworkPolicy egress restrictions, external Vault placement, and namespace-scoped RBAC on Secrets)

option_description: Defines the privilege scope of the kubeconfig or service account credential that is potentially exposed or stored in non-isolated zones. 'cluster_admin' represents full cluster-wide administrative control (equivalent to cluster-admin ClusterRole). 'broad_namespace' represents write access across multiple or all namespaces without full cluster admin. 'namespace_scoped' represents access limited to specific namespaces. 'read_only' represents access restricted to read operations only.
security_impact: The Rego policy gates 'kubeconfig_credential_not_isolated_by_zone' on credential_scope being 'cluster_admin' or 'broad_namespace' — both in combination with unsafe storage zones and workload-zone credential store access. This scope determines the blast radius of a credential theft event: cluster_admin scope gives an attacker complete control over all cluster resources, all namespaces, and the ability to create new ClusterRoleBindings to maintain persistence. broad_namespace scope enables lateral movement across multiple tenant namespaces and potential privilege escalation through RBAC manipulation. Lower scopes (namespace_scoped, read_only) do not trigger this exposure because their compromise does not collapse the control plane trust boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify the user or service account referenced in the kubeconfig and retrieve all ClusterRoleBindings and RoleBindings associated with it to determine privilege scope.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.users[0].name}' && kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq --arg user "$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.users[0].name}')" '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name == $user) | {binding: .metadata.name, roleRef: .roleRef}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ClusterRoleBindings referencing the credential's user/SA; roleRef of 'cluster-admin' confirms cluster_admin scope; custom roles require further inspection to classify as broad_namespace or namespace_scoped.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For service account tokens, determine the associated ClusterRole or Role and assess whether it grants cluster-admin, broad-namespace, namespace-scoped, or read-only access.
how_to_obtain.command: SA=<service-account-name>; NS=<namespace>; kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq --arg sa "$SA" --arg ns "$NS" '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | .kind == "ServiceAccount" and .name == $sa and .namespace == $ns) | .roleRef'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: roleRef entries showing the bound ClusterRole name; 'cluster-admin' maps to cluster_admin scope; roles with wildcard resources across many namespaces map to broad_namespace.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use kubectl auth can-i with impersonation to systematically verify whether a credential can perform cluster-admin-level operations.
how_to_obtain.command: CRED_USER=<kubeconfig-user>; kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --as=$CRED_USER && kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --as=$CRED_USER -n kube-system && kubectl auth can-i create clusterrolebindings --as=$CRED_USER
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'yes' to all verbs and resources indicates cluster_admin scope; 'yes' only within specific namespaces indicates broad_namespace or namespace_scoped; 'no' to write operations indicates read_only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the kubeconfig file itself to identify the user or service account, then cross-reference against RBAC definitions to classify the privilege scope.
how_to_obtain.command: cat ~/.kube/config | grep -A5 'users:' && kubectl get clusterrolebinding cluster-admin -o json | jq '.subjects'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: User or service account name from kubeconfig; cross-reference with cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding subjects list to confirm cluster_admin scope, or inspect other bindings for scope classification.

typical_values: cluster_admin (common for CI/CD pipeline kubeconfigs and initial cluster setup credentials)
broad_namespace (typical for GitOps operators like ArgoCD or Flux with multi-namespace deployment rights)
namespace_scoped (appropriate for application-specific service accounts with deployment rights in a single namespace)
read_only (typical for monitoring agents like Prometheus or audit tools)

option_description: Controls whether a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resource explicitly denies or limits workload pod/namespace access to control plane ports (6443 for API server, 2379/2380 for etcd, 10259 for kube-scheduler, 10257 for kube-controller-manager). This is an in-cluster software-defined network enforcement layer.
security_impact: The Rego rule control_plane_ingress_not_restricted_by_network_policy fires when BOTH network_policy_restricts_control_plane_ingress AND external_firewall_restricts_control_plane_ingress are false. Without this control, any compromised pod can directly reach control plane ports, bypassing logical authn/authz through network-level attacks such as credential replay, TLS downgrade, or exploitation of unauthenticated endpoints. This supports MITRE T1599 (Network Boundary Bridging) and T1562.007 (Disable or Modify Cloud Firewall).

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all NetworkPolicy resources across all namespaces and filter for egress rules targeting control plane ports. Review policyTypes and egress blocks.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.egress != null) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, egress: .spec.egress}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policies with egress rules that explicitly deny or limit traffic to ports 6443, 2379, 2380, 10259, 10257. Absence of such rules confirms the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search specifically for NetworkPolicy egress rules blocking or restricting the API server port 6443 across all workload namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | jq '[.items[] | select(.spec.egress[]?.ports[]?.port? == 6443 or .spec.egress[]?.ports[]?.port? == 2379)]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-empty list confirms egress rules exist for those ports. An empty array means no explicit control plane port restrictions exist via NetworkPolicy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check if the CNI plugin in use supports NetworkPolicy enforcement. Some CNIs (e.g., Flannel without Calico) silently ignore policies, making the attribute false even if policies exist.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave|antrea|canal'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of Calico, Cilium, Weave, Antrea, or Canal confirms NetworkPolicy enforcement is active. If only kubenet or Flannel (standalone) is present, policies are not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API directly for NetworkPolicy resources and inspect spec.egress rules for port targeting.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $(kubectl get secret -n kube-system $(kubectl get sa default -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.secrets[0].name}') -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d)" https://localhost:6443/apis/networking.k8s.io/v1/networkpolicies?limit=500 | jq '.items[].spec.egress'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Egress blocks listing port 6443, 2379, 2380, 10257, or 10259 as denied or restricted destinations confirm the attribute is true.

typical_values: false (default — most clusters lack explicit control plane egress restrictions)
true (hardened environments using Calico or Cilium with explicit deny-egress-to-control-plane policies)

option_description: Controls whether an external firewall layer — such as a cloud provider security group (AWS SG, GCP firewall rule, Azure NSG), VPC ACL, or host-level iptables/nftables ruleset — enforces deny or restrict rules preventing pod/node CIDRs from reaching API server (6443), etcd (2379/2380), scheduler (10259), and controller-manager (10257) ports on control plane nodes.
security_impact: The Rego rule control_plane_ingress_not_restricted_by_network_policy fires when both this attribute and network_policy_restricts_control_plane_ingress are false. External firewall enforcement is the defense-in-depth layer that operates below the Kubernetes control plane, providing network zone separation even if cluster-level policies are misconfigured or bypassed. Without it, attackers on the node network can directly contact etcd (T1040 Network Sniffing, T1599 Network Boundary Bridging) or the API server from compromised nodes or pods that escape CNI policy enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On AWS, retrieve the security groups attached to control plane nodes and list their inbound rules. Verify that pod and node CIDRs are not granted access to ports 6443, 2379, 2380, 10257, 10259.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=tag:kubernetes.io/cluster/${CLUSTER_NAME},Values=owned --query 'SecurityGroups[*].{ID:GroupId,Name:GroupName,Ingress:IpPermissions}' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Ingress rules should show that only control-plane-to-control-plane CIDR or bastion CIDR has access to ports 2379/2380. Pod CIDR blocks (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8) should be absent or explicitly denied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux control plane nodes, inspect iptables INPUT chain rules to determine whether pod or node subnet traffic to control plane ports is blocked.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v --line-numbers | grep -E '6443|2379|2380|10259|10257'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DROP or REJECT rules applied before ACCEPT rules for those ports against pod CIDR sources confirm host-level firewall restriction is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On GCP, list firewall rules for the cluster's network and check whether control plane ports are restricted to specific source ranges.
how_to_obtain.command: gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter="network=${NETWORK_NAME}" --format=json | jq '.[] | select(.allowed[]?.ports[]? | contains("6443") or contains("2379"))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules permitting ports 6443 or 2379 should list only control plane node IPs or management CIDRs as sourceRanges, not pod or node pool CIDRs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS Console, navigate to EC2 > Security Groups, filter by cluster tag, and inspect inbound rules on the control plane security group. Verify no rules permit pod subnet CIDRs on ports 6443, 2379, 2380, 10257, or 10259.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → EC2 → Security Groups → Filter by tag 'kubernetes.io/cluster/<cluster-name>' → Select control plane SG → Inbound Rules tab
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Inbound rules show only trusted management CIDRs or other control-plane nodes for administrative ports. Pod/node CIDRs absent from these rules.

typical_values: false (common in self-managed clusters without explicit firewall hardening)
true (managed Kubernetes services like EKS, GKE, AKS that isolate control plane nodes in provider-managed VPCs with restrictive security groups)

option_description: Represents the audit log verbosity level assigned to sensitive control plane resources — specifically secrets, clusterrolebindings, and pods/exec subresource — within the Kubernetes audit policy file. Valid values are None (no logging), Metadata (only HTTP metadata), Request (metadata plus request body), and RequestResponse (full request and response bodies).
security_impact: The Rego rule audit_log_gap_at_control_plane_boundary fires when this value is None or Metadata (when audit logging is otherwise active). A level of None means boundary-crossing events such as secret reads and RBAC escalations are completely invisible. Metadata captures only who made the call and when, but not what data was accessed — insufficient to detect credential harvesting (T1552.001) or RBAC manipulation (T1098.006). Request or RequestResponse is required for meaningful forensic coverage of control plane boundary crossings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the audit policy file path from the API server static pod manifest and then inspect the rules that apply to secrets, clusterrolebindings, and pods/exec resources.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep 'audit-policy-file' && cat $(cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep -oP '(?<=--audit-policy-file=)\S+') | grep -A5 -B5 -E 'secrets|clusterrolebindings|exec'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules with 'resources: [{group: "", resources: ["secrets"]}]' or similar, showing a 'level' field of Request or RequestResponse for a secure configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Directly inspect the audit policy YAML file referenced by --audit-policy-file. Look for rules matching secrets, clusterrolebindings, or pods subresource exec, and record their 'level' field values.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A 10 'secrets\|clusterrolebindings\|exec' /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each matching rule block should show 'level: Request' or 'level: RequestResponse'. Values of 'None' or 'Metadata' indicate a logging gap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the kube-apiserver process arguments directly on the control plane node to find the policy file path, then evaluate its content.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -oP '(?<=--audit-policy-file=)\S+' | xargs -I{} cat {} | python3 -c "import sys,yaml; policy=yaml.safe_load(sys.stdin); [print(r.get('level'), r.get('resources')) for r in policy.get('rules',[])]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output lines pairing level values with resource lists. Identify lines where secrets or clusterrolebindings are listed alongside None or Metadata.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Validate the effective audit log level by examining existing audit log entries for secret access events. If no request body appears in entries for GET /api/v1/namespaces/default/secrets, the level is Metadata or lower.
how_to_obtain.command: grep '"resource":"secrets"' /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | head -5 | jq '{level: .level, verb: .verb, responseObject: .responseObject}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries with 'level: RequestResponse' and populated responseObject fields confirm adequate logging. Entries with null responseObject and level Metadata indicate a gap.

typical_values: None (default when no explicit rule targets these resources and a catch-all None rule exists)
Metadata (common baseline audit policies that capture event metadata but not payloads)
Request (recommended minimum for compliance-oriented environments)
RequestResponse (high-assurance environments requiring full payload capture for forensics)

option_description: Indicates whether the Kubernetes API server has been started with either --audit-log-path (file-based audit logging) or --audit-webhook-config-file (webhook-based forwarding to an external SIEM or log aggregator) flags set to non-empty, non-null values. This is the prerequisite for any audit logging to occur at all.
security_impact: The Rego rule audit_log_gap_at_control_plane_boundary fires unconditionally when this attribute is false, regardless of policy file configuration. Without an audit log destination, all boundary-crossing events — secret reads, RBAC binding creation, privileged pod exec — are completely unrecorded. This directly enables T1562.008 (Disable or Modify Cloud Logs) and T1562.012 (Disable or Modify Linux Audit System) by leaving no forensic record. Even a well-crafted audit policy is inert without a configured output destination.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the kube-apiserver static pod manifest on the control plane node for the presence of --audit-log-path or --audit-webhook-config-file arguments.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'audit-log-path|audit-webhook-config-file' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines containing '--audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log' or '--audit-webhook-config-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-webhook.yaml' confirm the attribute is true. No output means audit logging is not configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the running kube-apiserver process arguments directly to check for audit output configuration regardless of what the manifest file shows.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E 'audit-log-path|audit-webhook-config-file'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-empty output with a valid path value confirms audit output is configured. Empty output means the running API server has no audit destination.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On managed Kubernetes platforms (EKS), check whether audit logging is enabled in the cluster configuration via the AWS CLI.
how_to_obtain.command: aws eks describe-cluster --name ${CLUSTER_NAME} --query 'cluster.logging.clusterLogging[?enabled==`true`].types' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output including 'audit' in the enabled types array confirms audit log path is configured via the managed control plane. Absence of 'audit' means the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the kube-apiserver configuration file (if using --config flag instead of individual flags) for auditLog or auditWebhook stanzas.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'auditLog\|auditWebhook' /etc/kubernetes/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration stanzas with non-empty path values under auditLog.path or a valid auditWebhook.configFile path confirm the attribute is true.

typical_values: false (common in development/test clusters and some managed offerings with audit logging disabled by default)
true (production clusters following CIS Kubernetes Benchmark, and managed services like GKE where audit logging is on by default)

option_description: Indicates whether the Kubernetes API server is started with the --audit-policy-file flag pointing to a readable, valid YAML file defining structured audit rules. Without this flag, the API server applies no fine-grained audit filtering — either logging nothing or using an implicit catch-all that cannot target specific sensitive resources.
security_impact: The Rego rule audit_log_gap_at_control_plane_boundary fires when audit_log_path_configured is true but this attribute is false, because a log destination without a policy file means the API server logs with no granularity — typically only a minimal default. Without a policy file, operators cannot ensure that secrets, clusterrolebindings, and pods/exec are logged at Request or RequestResponse level, leaving those boundary-crossing events under-recorded. This contributes to T1562.008 and T1562.012 risk by creating exploitable gaps in forensic coverage even when logging infrastructure exists.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the kube-apiserver static pod manifest for the --audit-policy-file flag and verify the referenced file exists and is readable.
how_to_obtain.command: POLICY_FILE=$(grep -oP '(?<=--audit-policy-file=)\S+' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml); echo "Flag value: $POLICY_FILE"; test -r "$POLICY_FILE" && echo 'File readable: true' || echo 'File readable: false'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing a non-empty file path and 'File readable: true' confirms the attribute is true. Empty flag value or unreadable path means the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the audit policy file is syntactically valid YAML with the expected apiVersion and kind fields.
how_to_obtain.command: cat $(grep -oP '(?<=--audit-policy-file=)\S+' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml) | python3 -c "import sys,yaml; p=yaml.safe_load(sys.stdin); print('apiVersion:', p.get('apiVersion'), 'kind:', p.get('kind'), 'rules:', len(p.get('rules',[])))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing 'apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1 kind: Policy rules: <N>' where N > 0 confirms a valid structured audit policy file is present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the running API server process to confirm the --audit-policy-file flag is active in the current process (not just the manifest).
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | tr ' ' '\n' | grep 'audit-policy-file'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A line containing '--audit-policy-file=/path/to/policy.yaml' confirms the attribute is true in the running process.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On GKE or AKS where the control plane is managed, verify audit policy presence through the cloud provider's API or CLI.
how_to_obtain.command: gcloud container clusters describe ${CLUSTER_NAME} --zone=${ZONE} --format=json | jq '.loggingConfig.componentConfig.enableComponents'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output including 'APISERVER' in enabled components confirms the managed control plane has audit policy active. Absence means audit policy file is not configured.

typical_values: false (default in kubeadm clusters if audit policy was not explicitly provided during init)
true (clusters bootstrapped with CIS-compliant tooling, kops with audit config, or managed services like GKE Autopilot)

option_description: Indicates whether kube-scheduler or kube-controller-manager components have their --bind-address flag set to a non-loopback address such as 0.0.0.0 or a specific node IP, causing their health check (/healthz), liveness (/livez), and metrics (/metrics) HTTP/HTTPS endpoints to be accessible from interfaces beyond localhost. The default secure configuration binds to 127.0.0.1.
security_impact: The Rego rule scheduler_and_controller_manager_unauthenticated_endpoints fires when BOTH bind_address_non_loopback is true AND authentication_disabled_on_endpoint is true. Binding to 0.0.0.0 exposes these endpoints to the node network and potentially the pod network, providing unauthenticated reconnaissance surface (T1613 Container and Resource Discovery). Exposed scheduler metrics reveal node capacity, pending pod queues, and scheduling latency. Controller manager metrics expose reconciliation state and resource counts — information directly useful for targeted cluster attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager static pod manifests for the --bind-address flag value.
how_to_obtain.command: grep 'bind-address' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing '--bind-address=127.0.0.1' indicate secure configuration (attribute false). Lines showing '0.0.0.0', a node IP, or absence of the flag (which may default to 0.0.0.0 in older versions) indicate the attribute is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check running process arguments for both components to confirm the actual bind address in use, independent of manifest configuration.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep -E 'kube-scheduler|kube-controller-manager' | tr ' ' '\n' | grep 'bind-address'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Values of 127.0.0.1 or ::1 indicate the attribute is false. Values of 0.0.0.0, a routable IP, or no output (older binaries may default to 0.0.0.0) indicate the attribute is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a workload pod or node network segment, attempt to reach the scheduler and controller manager metrics endpoints to confirm whether they are reachable beyond localhost.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk --max-time 3 https://<control-plane-node-ip>:10259/healthz && echo 'SCHEDULER REACHABLE' || echo 'BLOCKED'; curl -sk --max-time 3 https://<control-plane-node-ip>:10257/healthz && echo 'CONTROLLER-MANAGER REACHABLE' || echo 'BLOCKED'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection timeout or refused from non-localhost confirms the attribute is false. A successful response ('ok') confirms the endpoint is exposed (attribute true).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check ss or netstat on the control plane node to see which interfaces ports 10259 and 10257 are bound to.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing '127.0.0.1:10259' and '127.0.0.1:10257' confirm loopback-only binding (attribute false). Lines showing '0.0.0.0:10259' or a node IP confirm non-loopback binding (attribute true).

typical_values: false (Kubernetes 1.20+ defaults to 127.0.0.1 for secure port binding)
true (legacy clusters pre-1.17 or misconfigured clusters where 0.0.0.0 was set explicitly for monitoring agent compatibility)

option_description: Indicates whether the health/metrics endpoints of kube-scheduler or kube-controller-manager have authentication bypassed through one of three mechanisms: (1) --authentication-kubeconfig flag is absent or empty, preventing the component from verifying bearer tokens; (2) --authentication-skip-lookup=true is set, causing all token validation to be skipped; or (3) the deprecated insecure --port flag is set to a non-zero value, enabling an HTTP endpoint with no authentication at all.
security_impact: The Rego rule scheduler_and_controller_manager_unauthenticated_endpoints requires BOTH bind_address_non_loopback AND authentication_disabled_on_endpoint to be true. Authentication bypass on these endpoints means any network-reachable client can query /metrics without presenting credentials, exposing cluster topology, workload scheduling patterns, and resource usage (T1613 Container and Resource Discovery). The deprecated --port mechanism additionally exposes these endpoints over plain HTTP, enabling passive interception (T1040). Combined with a non-loopback bind address, this creates a complete unauthenticated reconnaissance surface at the control plane boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager manifests for missing or empty --authentication-kubeconfig, presence of --authentication-skip-lookup=true, or non-zero --port.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'authentication-kubeconfig|authentication-skip-lookup|^\s*-\s*--port' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of '--authentication-kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf' and absence of '--authentication-skip-lookup=true' and '--port=0' (or non-zero port) indicates secure config. Missing kubeconfig flag or skip-lookup=true means authentication is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect running process arguments for all three authentication-disabling conditions simultaneously.
how_to_obtain.command: for proc in kube-scheduler kube-controller-manager; do echo "=== $proc ==="; ps aux | grep $proc | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E 'authentication-kubeconfig|authentication-skip-lookup|--port='; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: For each component: '--authentication-kubeconfig' should be present with a non-empty path. '--authentication-skip-lookup' should be absent or false. '--port' should be 0 or absent. Any deviation means authentication is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to reach the metrics endpoint of the controller manager without credentials from a node that has network access. An HTTP 200 without a token indicates authentication is disabled.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk --max-time 5 https://127.0.0.1:10257/metrics 2>&1 | head -3
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An HTTP 401 Unauthorized response confirms authentication is enforced (attribute false). An HTTP 200 with metrics data, or a successful response to the plain HTTP port (curl http://127.0.0.1:10252/metrics), confirms authentication is disabled (attribute true).

how_to_obtain.instruction: If components use a --config file instead of flags, inspect the componentConfig YAML for the authentication section.
how_to_obtain.command: CONFIG_FILE=$(grep -oP '(?<=--config=)\S+' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml); cat "$CONFIG_FILE" | grep -A5 'authentication:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A block showing 'authentication: webhook: enabled: true' and a non-empty 'kubeconfig' path confirms authentication is active. 'enabled: false' or absent block means authentication is disabled (attribute true).

typical_values: false (Kubernetes 1.20+ enables authentication by default when --authentication-kubeconfig is provided via kubeadm-generated manifests)
true (legacy clusters using --port=10252/10251 for monitoring compatibility, or manually configured clusters missing the authentication-kubeconfig flag)
